CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of kidney stones.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male presenting with a one-week history of right-sided flank pain that began suddenly while working in the barn moving hay. He initially attributed the pain to his work activity, but the acute onset was accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. He presented to his PCP who ordered a CT scan that confirmed the presence of a kidney stone. The pain radiated almost to the groin but did not extend the full distance. Since the initial episode, he has experienced intermittent pain that is less intense and shorter in duration than the initial presentation. He denies hematuria. He has been straining his urine as instructed and has not observed any stone fragments. He denies fever or dysuria.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for initial diaphoresis and nausea associated with acute flank pain. Denies hematuria, fever, or dysuria. No other systemic symptoms reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No prior kidney stones. Denies other significant past medical history.

MEDICATIONS
No current medications listed.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Father with history of recurrent kidney stones.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works with horses and performs manual labor including hay moving.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Normal, no fever. Blood pressure and heart rate within normal limits. Abdomen: Soft, no tenderness to palpation, no rebound or guarding. CVA tenderness appreciated on the right side consistent with kidney inflammation from stone.

RESULTS
CT scan: 0.5 cm stone located in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis. Pending: BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right ureteral kidney stone (0.5 cm, proximal right ureter), uncomplicated. Plan includes: (1) Increase fluid intake to facilitate passage of stone; (2) Oxycodone 5 mg every 6-8 hours for pain management with acetaminophen for breakthrough pain; (3) Continue urine straining; (4) Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture to rule out infection; (5) Consider antibiotics based on urinalysis results if infection present; (6) Follow-up in 1-2 weeks; (7) Discuss lithotripsy as alternative treatment option if stone does not pass within 1-2 weeks.
